title: Union with Scotland Act 1706, ARTICLE I - The Kingdoms United; Ensigns Armorial
citation: 6 Ann. c. 11 (1706 c. 11); noted in the official text as 'Chapter VIII. 5 & 6 Ann. in the Common printed Editions'
legislature: Parliament of England (ratifying the Articles of Union)
quotation: That the two Kingdoms of England and Scotland shall upon the First day of May which shall be in the year One thousand seven hundred and seven and for ever after be united into one Kingdom by the name of Great Britain
territorial_wording: England; Scotland; one Kingdom by the name of Great Britain
interpretation: The constitutional proposition that from 1 May 1707 England and Scotland are one kingdom. This is the authority for treating the whole main island as a single territorial actor rather than as two. It says nothing about where any coastline runs.
source: legislation.gov.uk (The National Archives, Open Government Licence)

title: An Act for erecting, maintaining and supporting a Light House on the Island of Little Cumray in the County of Bute, at the Mouth of the River Clyde, in North Britain; and for rendering the Navigation in the Frith and River of Clyde more safe and commodious
quotation: on the Island of Little Cumray in the County of Bute, at the Mouth of the River Clyde, in North Britain
territorial_wording: County of Bute; River Clyde; North Britain (the post-Union statutory term for Scotland)
interpretation: In the snapshot year the Parliament of Great Britain legislates for a named place in Scotland, calling it North Britain. Read together with the England act below, one legislature is exercising territorial authority across both former kingdoms.
source: legislation.gov.uk (The National Archives, Open Government Licence)

title: An Act for regulating the Proceedings in Personal Actions in the Courts Baron of the Manors of Sheffield and Ecclesall, in the County of York
quotation: the Manors of Sheffield and Ecclesall, in the County of York
interpretation: The same 1756 Parliament legislating for a named place in England, in the same session as the Bute act. The pair is the point: one authority, both halves of the island.
source: legislation.gov.uk (The National Archives, Open Government Licence)

title: Sheriffs Act 1755, CHAPTER XV - An Act to supply the Defects of an Act passed in the eleventh Year of the Reign of her late Majesty Queen Anne, intituled, An Act for explaining and amending several Statutes for prohibiting Under-Sheriffs and Sheriffs Clerks from officiating as Sub-Sheriffs or Sheriffs Clerks more than one Year
quotation: That from and after the first day of May, which shall be in the year of our Lord one thousand seven hundred and fifty six, no sub-sheriff or sheriffs clerk shall take any more than their legal fees ... which said penalty shall be ... estreated into his Majesty's Exchequer
territorial_wording: sub-sheriffs and sheriffs clerks; the court out of which such writ issued; his Majesty's Exchequer [of Ireland]
interpretation: The strongest Irish datum available. A statute of the Irish Parliament whose operative clause takes effect on 1 MAY 1756 - three months before the snapshot instant - regulating county sheriffs' officers throughout Ireland and enforced through Irish courts and the Irish Exchequer. Administration actually running on the ground at the snapshot, not a claim.
source: electronic Irish Statute Book (eISB), Office of the Attorney General, Pre-1922 Legislation

title: Cork Infirmary Act 1751
exact_locator: Statute Law Revision Act 2007 (Ireland), Schedule 1, entry '1751 (25 Geo. 2) c. 23 / Cork Infirmary / Cork Infirmary Act 1751'
interpretation: A second, place-specific Irish act still retained in force by the Irish State, showing the Irish Parliament legislating for a named place inside Ireland in the years around the snapshot.
source: electronic Irish Statute Book (eISB), Office of the Attorney General, Pre-1922 Legislation

title: Union with Ireland Act 1800, Article First
quotation: Great Britain and Ireland shall upon Jan. 1, 1801, be united into one kingdom
interpretation: Recorded precisely so it can NEVER be applied to 1756. Great Britain and Ireland become one kingdom only from 1 January 1801, forty-five years after the snapshot. At 1756-08-01 they are two kingdoms under one crown, and no territorial merge may be derived from that shared crown.
source: legislation.gov.uk (The National Archives, Open Government Licence)
